title: The Ten Commandments
note:
Built from the curriculum photographs in Drive’s Beginner → Chapter 17 → “01 - Curriculum Source”: four pages, p.77 (title, prayer, Bible portion), p.78 (the lesson), p.79 (“Tell the Answers” and “Fill in the Blanks”) and p.82 (My Decision, the song line, the Memory Verse and the Concluding Prayer).

**p.80 and p.81 are not in Drive.** The folder was paginated to the end and holds exactly four photographs, and the page numbers jump from 79 to 82. Nothing in this chapter depends on them — all four printed questions are on p.79 and every answer is in the lesson on p.78 — but by the shape of this book two pages is more than an activity page, and they may well carry the ten commandments listed out in full, which this chapter summarises rather than lists. Worth a photograph if they do.

**The workbook’s answer and the lesson’s answer disagree on question 2, and the games follow the lesson.** “Why did Moses climb up to the mountain.?” is answered on p.78 by “On the mountain God gave Moses instructions and directions which the Israelites were to practice in their life and in their journey.” But p.79’s “Fill in the Blanks” 2 offers only “to take rest” or “to pray”, and the lesson says neither. The second game uses the lesson’s reason as its correct answer and keeps “To rest from the journey” as a wrong option, so a child working from that page finds it here and finds it wrong. This is an editorial question for the teacher.

**There is no `song`.** p.82’s “Learn to sing” says only “(Sing a suitable English song)” — a stage direction to the teacher rather than a song, in the same way Chapters 12 and 14 printed a stage direction where a prayer goes. There is nothing to carry, so the field is absent rather than filled with the instruction.

`prayer` carries the Concluding Prayer from p.82. The opening prayer on p.77 is printed in full as well, but the schema holds one and the closing one is what the rest of this class carries.

**Artwork.** Ten panels and both covers came from Drive’s “04 - Story Artwork”, all twelve distinct by SHA-256, the folder enumerated by exact filename rather than by paging. The twenty-four text cards this chapter first shipped with are gone rather than reconciled, which is what happened to Beginner Chapters 5 to 16 and to Primary 1 to 3. Each card is now a picture with `alt` describing the scene and quoting what is lettered on it.

Panel 8 is 941×1671, one pixel short of the canonical 941×1672. Converted without distortion and nothing resized it.

**Only three of the ten panels can be shelf cards, so one game has none.** Panels 1, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10 all have a speech bubble cut mid-sentence by the square centre crop — at the size a card actually prints, about 165px, a cut bubble reads as broken text rather than as a picture. Panel 9 crops cleanly but letters “Jesus taught us to love God and our neighbors”, which is the fourth game’s answer, and the shelf is read whole before any game is played, so it is barred from every card and not just that one. The third game goes without, for the reason given in its note.

cover.note: Both drawn and imported, both at the canonical sizes — 941×1672 portrait and 1672×941 landscape.

story.alt: A boy sits cross-legged on his bedroom rug with a toy truck and building blocks around him, Halo glowing beside him. The boy asks, “Halo, why do we have rules?” and Halo answers, “That’s a good question! Let’s discover why God gave His people commandments.”

The boy and his little sister kneel on the floor building a tower out of coloured blocks together, Halo floating above them. Halo says, “Rules can help us do what is good and loving.” and the boy says, “I want to learn God’s rules!”

Moses stands at the front of a crowd of his people with his staff, tents pitched behind them and the bare rock of Mount Sinai rising into the sky. The caption reads, “After three months of their journey, the Israelites reached the wilderness near Mount Sinai.”

Moses climbs the mountain path alone, his staff raised, looking up, with the whole camp and its tents spread out small on the plain below him. The caption reads, “Moses climbed Mount Sinai to receive God’s instructions.”

Near the summit, lightning in dark cloud on one side and a burst of golden light on the other, Moses kneels with his hands open. The caption reads, “God gave Moses instructions for the Israelites to follow in their lives.” The light says, “These are My commandments for My people.” and Moses answers, “Yes, Lord! I will listen and obey.”

Moses stands in the light holding two stone tablets, one numbered I to V and the other VI to X in Hebrew lettering. The caption reads, “God gave Moses ten important commandments and wrote them on two stone tablets.” The light says, “These are My commandments for My people. Follow them and live the way I have shown you.”

Moses holds both tablets up at the foot of the mountain, the heads of the people in front of him. The caption reads, “Moses came down the mountain and showed the people God’s commandments.” Moses says, “These are God’s commandments. Let us obey Him and live the way He wants us to.”

Moses holds one tablet against his chest and opens his other hand to the crowd. The caption reads, “Moses read God’s commandments to the people.” He says, “You shall love God with all your heart. You shall be kind, honest, and treat others with love. Do not steal, do not lie, and always do what is right.”

Back in the bedroom, the boy rests his chin on his hand beside a globe and a shelf of books, Halo glowing by him. The caption reads, “God wants us to understand and follow His commandments every day.” The boy asks, “So I should love God and the people around me?” and Halo answers, “Yes! Jesus taught us to love God and our neighbors.”

The boy sits at his desk with his eyes closed and his hands folded over an open book, Halo beside him. The caption reads, “God wants us to follow His commandments with devotion. We can show our love for God and our friends every day.” He says, “I will love God!” and “I will love my friends!” Halo answers, “That’s a wonderful decision! When we love God and others, we are following His commandments.”

curriculum.source: Beginners Mar Thoma Vol-1, Chapter 17 “The Ten Commandments”, p.79 — “Tell the Answers”
curriculum.note: All four questions transcribed from the printed page, punctuation included — the stray full stops before the question marks (“journey.?”, “mountain.?”, “given.?”, “Commandments.?”) are the book’s, not typos here. The four “Fill in the Blanks” on the same page are not recorded as questions: three of them restate questions 1, 3 and 4, and the fourth offers two answers the lesson does not give, which the chapter note sets out.

questions.question: Where did Israel reach after completing three months journey.?
questions.objective: Remember that Israel reached the desert near Mount Sinai.
questions.answer: The desert near Mount Sinai. “After three months of that long journey, they reached the desert near Mount Sinai.” (p.78)

questions.question: Why did Moses climb up to the mountain.?
questions.objective: Remember that God gave Moses instructions and directions on the mountain.
questions.answer: Because God gave him instructions there. “On the mountain God gave Moses instructions and directions which the Israelites were to practice in their life and in their journey.” (p.78)

questions.question: How many Commandments has God given.?
questions.objective: Remember that God gave ten commandments.
questions.answer: Ten. “There were ten important points… They are known as the ten Commandments.” (p.78)

questions.question: What did Jesus teach about the summary of ten Commandments.?
questions.objective: Remember that Jesus summed them up as loving God and loving your neighbour.
questions.answer: Two commandments — love God, and love your neighbour. “1. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind and with all your strength. 2. Love your neighbor as you love yourself.” (p.78)

games.title: To Mount Sinai
games.objective: Remember that after three months the people of Israel reached the desert near Mount Sinai.
games.note:
The lesson opens by recapping chapters this class has already had — Egypt, Moses, the manna, the pillar of cloud and fire — before it reaches Sinai, so the first game is that recap put back in order. Every step is from p.78’s own first sentences. It answers question 1 by arriving at Sinai rather than by naming it from a list.

Shelf picture panel-03. Moses at the head of his people with the tents pitched and Mount Sinai behind. The caption — “After three months of their journey, the Israelites reached the wilderness near Mount Sinai” — is cropped away, so the card carries no lettering. It shows the arrival, which is where this sequence ends, but a picture cannot give away an *order*: all five steps are already on the board and the task is putting them in line.

games.title: Up the Mountain
games.objective: Remember that Moses climbed the mountain because God gave him instructions there.

interactions.prompt: Why did Moses climb the mountain?
interactions.hint: God had something to give him.

games.note:
**This game uses the lesson’s answer, not the workbook’s.** p.78 says “On the mountain God gave Moses instructions and directions”, so that is the correct option. p.79’s “Fill in the Blanks” 2 offers “to take rest / to pray”, neither of which the lesson says — see the chapter note. “To rest from the journey” is kept as a wrong option precisely because it is the workbook’s other choice, and a child who has been given that page should find it here and find it wrong.

Shelf picture panel-04. Moses climbing the path alone with the camp small below him. No lettering survives the crop, and what the picture shows is the question rather than the answer: he is climbing, which is what is being asked about, and nothing here says why.

games.title: Ten on Two Tablets
games.objective: Remember that God gave ten commandments, written on two stone tablets.

interactions.prompt: Match the numbers to the story.

games.note:
Three numbers and a name, all from p.78. “Three → Months of the journey” is there so that ten and two are not the only numbers on the board — a child who can see there are exactly two numbers can pair them without remembering either. “Moses → Who climbed the mountain” does the same job for the other side.

**No shelf picture, deliberately.** Every panel that draws the commandments draws two tablets with ten numerals on them — 6, 7 and 8 all do — and this game’s two answers are “Ten → how many commandments” and “Two → how many stone tablets”. A card that shows the answer is no better than one that letters it, which is the rule Chapter 16 applied to its altar panels. Of the ten panels only 2, 3 and 4 survive the square crop with their lettering whole; 9 crops clean but letters the fourth game’s answer, so it is barred from the shelf entirely. That leaves three cards for four games, and this is the game whose picture could not have been honest anyway. It renders as it did before the artwork arrived.

games.title: What Jesus Taught
games.objective: Remember that Jesus summed up the ten commandments as loving God and loving your neighbour.

interactions.prompt: What did Jesus say to love?
interactions.hint: He named two things to love.

games.note:
The lesson gives Jesus’ two commandments in full, so the question has an answer on the page. Both wrong options pair something real from this chapter with something else real from it — the mountain, Moses, the tablets — rather than inventing a plausible-sounding pair. The reveal then opens the two commandments themselves, four cards from p.78’s own wording, and answers nothing the game above it is marked on.

Shelf picture panel-02. The boy and his sister building together while Halo says rules help us do what is good and loving — the whole bubble survives the crop, and “I want to learn God’s rules!” is the chapter’s question rather than this game’s answer. Panel 9 is the obvious card for this game and is barred: it letters “Jesus taught us to love God and our neighbors”, which is the answer, and barred from the whole shelf rather than just from here — all four cards are read before any game is played.

practice.hint: It begins with something God gave.
practice.note: Stage 1, recognition. The wrong options are ordinary phrases rather than invented scripture, and they are deliberately near-misses on the shape of the word — law, land, light — because with a verse this short there is nothing else to tell apart.

practice.hint: It begins with what belongs to God.
practice.note: Stage 2, phrase ordering. Three chunks, broken where the sense breathes. The build checks that they spell the verse exactly.

Stage 3, the missing word. Generated by the Memory Verse agent’s Beginner ladder and used exactly as it came out.

It is the only stage 3 in this class with **two** options rather than three, and that is the verse’s doing rather than the agent’s. The agent builds its distractors from the verse’s own words, which is the rule that keeps a child from being asked to reject invented scripture. “Your law is my delight” is five words, and three of them are “your”, “is” and “my” — so once “law” is the answer there is exactly one other word in the whole verse that could stand beside it. Three options were not available without inventing one, and a fabricated option is worse than a short list. The band’s maxOptions is a ceiling, not a floor.

Stage 4, full reconstruction — five pieces where stage 2 had three, which is the whole of the difference between the two stages.

This is the one chapter in the class where the five pieces are **single words** rather than phrase chunks, and again it is the verse: it is five words long, so five chunks and five words are the same thing. Every other chapter breaks phrases because its verse is long enough to have phrases. The build checks that these five spell the verse exactly.

practice.prompt: Where does our verse come from?
practice.hint: The longest Psalm in the Bible.
practice.note:
Stage 5, the reference — recognised, not typed. `write-reference` asks for a keyboard, and a six-year-old spelling “Psalms 119:174(b)” is a typing test wearing a memory verse. Both distractors are references this child has just met: Psalm 133 was Chapter 15’s verse and Genesis 15 was Chapter 16’s.

The label reads “Psalm 119” where the book prints “Psalms 119:174(b)” — the same singular-for-plural edit as Chapters 14 and 15, so that the correct label is not the only plural among three singulars.

verse.note:
Read from p.82 through the Memory Verse agent: `--fetch --source-dir` over the four curriculum photographs, the supervised read, then `--from-extraction`.

Five stages in the shape Chapters 1 to 9 and 11 to 16 of this class use — recognise, order, fill, rebuild, place. Stage 3 is the agent’s own Beginner rung, unedited; the other four are built by hand on top of it.

**This is the shortest memory verse in the class — five words — and it bends two things that have held for every other chapter.** Stage 3 has two options rather than three, and stage 4 is single words rather than phrase chunks. Both notes below say why, and in both cases the alternative was to invent something the verse does not contain.

The reference is printed “Psalms 119:174(b)” on p.82, with the plural and the part letter, and is carried here exactly as printed. The “(b)” means the second half of the verse, which is why the text is a clause rather than a sentence.

Translation is unresolved, which is where every other chapter in this class stands.

No second opinion — the teacher’s editorial Sheet was not available for this run.

decision.statement: I will love God. I will love my Friends.
decision.note: The curriculum’s own My Decision from p.82, which is printed as two lines — “I will love God” and “I will love my Friends” — joined into one statement because the field holds one. The capital F on “Friends” is the book’s. It is the chapter’s two commandments in a child’s own words.

prayer.text: Thank you Lord for helping us to learn about your Commandments. Help us to live according to your laws. Amen.
prayer.note: The Concluding Prayer from p.82, word for word.

celebration.message: Jesus put all ten into two: love God, love your neighbour.
celebration.note: The turn of the chapter, from p.78. Ten commandments on two stone tablets is where the lesson starts; what it ends on is Jesus gathering all ten into two a six-year-old can hold.
